title: 50-30-20 Budget - Dev
description:
In this project, you will build a personal monthly budget using Google Sheets and the 50/30/20 budgeting rule. This rule suggests spending roughly 50% of your after-tax income on needs, 30% on wants, and 20% on savings and financial goals. You will choose a career, research a realistic salary, and then plan how you would spend your monthly take-home pay across those three categories.


Along the way, you will practice key spreadsheet skills including writing formulas, using functions, applying number formatting, and working with absolute cell references. By the end, you will have a working budget that calculates your income, tracks your spending, and shows whether your plan follows the 50/30/20 guideline. You will also reflect on what you learned about both spreadsheets and personal budgeting.

sections.title: Project Setup
sections.description: In this section, you will watch an introductory video, enter your personal scenario information, and set up the income values that power the rest of your spreadsheet. Getting these details right matters because every formula you build later depends on the numbers you enter here.

objectives.title: Watch Me
objectives.description: Watch the "Watch Me" video linked in cell D1. This video will introduce you to important GradeFlow features and show you exactly what you need to do to complete this task. You can also watch the task video(s) for step-by-step instructions.

resources.title: Vide01.01 Watch Me
resources.transcript_summary:
This video walks you through the Grade Flow platform so you know how to navigate the assignment. You'll learn that the left sidebar contains all your instructions: the dark green cards are section overviews and the lighter green cards are individual tasks. Gear icons mean the platform grades your work instantly when you click "Evaluate," while apple icons mean your teacher (or AI) will grade those later. You can toggle between "All," "Complete," and "Incomplete" tabs to track your progress.

The video also shows you the Google Sheets file you'll be working in and introduces the Resources tab, which contains helpful links including the Grade Flow Buddy AI and prompt frameworks you'll use throughout the project. Your first actual task is to rename the "Resource" tab to "Resources" (just add an "S"), then delete the Watch Me link from the spreadsheet. After evaluating, you'll earn your first points and move on to the next task.

resources.transcript_summary:
This video shows you how to enter your annual gross income and effective tax rate into the spreadsheet. You'll use Prompt 2 from the Resources tab, paste it into an AI tool, and fill in your career and location. The AI researches realistic salary ranges and calculates your effective tax rate, which averages together federal, state, and other taxes rather than just using the highest bracket.

Once you have your numbers, you enter the salary in cell C7 (formatted as currency) and the tax rate in cell C6 (formatted as a percentage). sections.title: Formulas
sections.description: In this section, you will write your first spreadsheet formulas to calculate your take-home pay. These formulas connect your income and tax data so that if you ever change your career or location, the entire budget updates automatically. Understanding how to build formulas that reference other cells is one of the most important spreadsheet skills you can develop.

objectives.title: Annual Net Pay
objectives.description:
In cell C8, write a formula that calculates your estimated annual net pay (income after taxes). Your formula must reference cells C6 and C7, use multiplication and subtraction operators, and include parentheses for the correct order of operations. Format the cell as currency.


EXAMPLE:

[Annual Gross Income] * (1-[Effective Tax Rate])

resources.title: Video2.01
resources.transcript_summary:
This video teaches you how to calculate your annual net pay (your income after taxes but before any other deductions). In cell C8, you write the formula =C7*(1-C6), which takes your annual gross income and multiplies it by the portion you keep after taxes. For example, if your tax rate is 32%, then 1 minus 0.32 equals 0.68, meaning you keep 68% of your gross income.

After entering the formula, you need to format cell C8 as currency. Then click Evaluate to earn your points. This is a straightforward formula task, but make sure you understand the math: you're multiplying income by (1 minus tax rate) to get your take-home pay.

objectives.title: Monthly Net Pay
objectives.description:
In cell C9, write a formula that calculates your estimated monthly net pay by dividing your Estimated Annual Net Pay by 12. Your formula must reference cell C8 and use the division operator. Format the cell as currency.


EXAMPLE:

[Estimated Annual Net Pay] / [Months in a Year]

resources.title: Video02.02
resources.transcript_summary: This video covers calculating your monthly net pay. The formula is simple: take your estimated annual net income (from the previous task) and divide it by 12. You write =C8/12 in the appropriate cell. This gives you the amount of cash you have each month to work with for your budget. Format the result as currency, evaluate, and move on. This number is the foundation for all three spending categories (needs, wants, and savings) in the 50/30/20 budget.

sections.title: Needs
sections.description: Needs are expenses you cannot avoid. These are the bills and costs required to live safely and maintain your basic responsibilities. In this section, you will research and list realistic monthly costs for essentials like housing, food, transportation, utilities, and insurance. You will also use a SUM function and write a formula to see what percentage of your income goes toward needs. The 50/30/20 rule suggests keeping this category at or below 50%.

Practice writing your own CTF Prompt to help you with the research. Watch the task video for step-by-step instructions.

resources.title: Video03.01
resources.transcript_summary:
This video starts the Needs section of your budget with housing, which must be listed as either "Rent" or "Mortgage." You need to research a realistic housing cost for your chosen location. The video demonstrates using a Context-Task-Format (CTF) prompt with an AI tool to find apartment prices. You write a prompt asking the AI to act as a cost-of-living expert and return apartment options with names, descriptions, and monthly rents within your price range.

After reviewing the AI results, you pick a realistic option and enter the housing type (like "Rent" or "One Bedroom") and the dollar amount into the spreadsheet. Make sure to format the dollar amount as currency before evaluating. The key takeaway is learning to write your own CTF prompts to research real costs rather than just guessing numbers.

resources.title: Video03.02
resources.transcript_summary:
This video shows you how to fill in seven needs for your monthly budget. Since you probably don't know every expense an adult has, the video teaches you how to use AI to help with research. You take a screenshot of the task requirements (or copy the text), paste it into an AI tool like Gemini, and ask the AI to write a CTF prompt for you. Then you take that generated prompt, fill in your personal details (job title, city, salary), and run it in another AI chat to get realistic monthly cost estimates for common needs.

This is a practical example of "applied AI skills," where you use AI to help you figure out what to ask AI. The video emphasizes that this process of using AI to write better prompts is a valuable real-world skill. You need to fill in seven needs with dollar amounts, make sure they're formatted as currency, and add notes to explain your choices.

objectives.description:

EXAMPLE:

resources.title: Video03.03
resources.transcript_summary:
This video teaches you how to write a SUM function to total up your needs expenses. In cell D27, you enter =SUM(C12:C26), which adds up all the values in that range. The video explains that functions are pre-written formulas that take inputs called "arguments." SUM takes a range of cells and adds them together. The important thing is to include the full range (C12 through C26) so that if you add more items later, they'll automatically be included in the total.

After writing the SUM formula, you must format the cell as currency. The video also shows what happens if your range is wrong: if the evaluator says your formula should be C12:C26 but yours says C12:C24, you need to double-click the cell and fix the range. Always check the hints and feedback after evaluating to make sure your formula covers the correct range.

objectives.description:

resources.title: Video03.04
resources.transcript_summary:
This video shows you how to calculate what percentage of your monthly net pay goes toward needs. In cell E27, you write a formula that divides your needs subtotal (D27) by your estimated monthly net pay (C9). You then format the result as a percentage. The video introduces absolute cell references: you place a dollar sign before the row number in C$9 so that when you copy this formula later to the wants and savings sections, it always points back to row 9 (your monthly net pay) instead of shifting down.

Without the dollar sign, copying the formula to a new location would change C9 to a different cell, giving you the wrong answer. With the absolute reference (C$9), the row stays locked no matter where you paste the formula. This is a critical concept you'll reuse throughout the rest of the project.

sections.title: Wants
sections.description: Wants are things you enjoy but could live without. This includes entertainment, dining out, subscriptions, hobbies, and other lifestyle choices. Budgeting for wants is not about cutting fun out of your life. It is about being intentional with your spending so you can enjoy things without falling behind on what matters. The 50/30/20 rule suggests keeping wants at or below 30%.

You need seven wants with dollar amounts formatted as currency. The video also suggests adding a few sentences about your personal interests so the AI gives you more relevant suggestions. Meta prompting (using AI to help you write better prompts) is highlighted as a powerful skill. Once your seven wants are entered and formatted, evaluate to get your points.

  1. Select cells D27and E27, and copy them.
  2. Select cells D45and E45, and paste.


If you want be build the formula manually, follow these instructions.

  1. In cell D45, use the SUM() function to add up all of your monthly want costs. Your formula should sum the range C30:C44. Format the cell as currency.


EXAMPLE:

SUM(value1)

resources.title: Video 04.03 & 04.04
resources.transcript_summary:
This video teaches you how to reuse formulas by copying and pasting them from the Needs section down to the Wants section. You highlight the subtotal and percentage cells from Needs (D27 and E27), copy them (Ctrl/Cmd+C), and paste them into the corresponding Wants cells. Because the SUM formula uses relative references, it automatically adjusts to add up the wants range instead of the needs range. The percentage formula also adjusts, but the absolute reference (C$9) stays locked on your monthly net pay, which is exactly what you want.

The video explains the difference clearly: relative references (like C12:C26) shift when you move the formula, so they adapt to whatever section you paste into. Absolute references (like C$9 with the dollar sign) stay fixed no matter where you paste. If you prefer not to copy and paste, you can also write each formula manually using the step-by-step instructions provided in the task. Either way, you'll get points for both tasks (04.03 and 04.04) once the formulas are correct.

sections.title: Financials
sections.description: Financial goals are how you build long-term security. This includes your emergency fund, retirement savings, debt payments, and other savings goals. Many people skip this category or treat it as optional, but building these habits early makes a significant difference over time. The 50/30/20 rule suggests putting at least 20% toward savings and financial goals.

objectives.title: % Monthly Net Pay
objectives.description:
In this task you'll learn how to copy, paste, and adjust cell formulas and formatting in other areas or your spreadsheet. Watch the task video(s) for step-by-step instructions and to learn why this method works in this situation.

  1. Select cells D45and E45, and copy them.
  2. Select cells D53and E53, and paste.


If you want be build the formula manually, follow these instructions.

  1. In cell E53, write a formula that divides your Financial Goals Subtotal (D53) by your Estimated Monthly Net Pay. Use the absolute row reference C$9. Format the cell as a percentage.


EXAMPLE:

[Financials Subtotal] / [Estimated Monthly Net Pay]

Cell E53 should display a number after your formula calculates. If you see an error, make sure D53 and C9 both contain values.

sections.title: Totals and Chart
sections.description: This section brings everything together. You will calculate your total monthly spending, find out how much money remains, and see whether your budget follows the 50/30/20 guideline. These totals give you the full picture of your financial plan and help you decide whether any adjustments are needed.

objectives.title: Total Spending
objectives.description:
In cell D55, write a formula that adds your three subtotals together: Needs Subtotal (D27), Wants Subtotal (D45), and Financial Goals Subtotal (D53). Use the addition operator. Format the cell as currency.


EXAMPLE:

[Needs Subtotal] + [Wants Subtotal] + [Financials Subtotal]

resources.title: Video 06.01
resources.transcript_summary: This is a quick task. You write a formula that adds up the three subtotals from your needs, wants, and savings sections. It's a simple cell reference formula with two plus signs: =D27+D45+D53 (or wherever your three subtotals are). Format the result as currency, evaluate, and you'll get all your points. This gives you your total monthly spending across all three budget categories.

evaluations.failure_message: Your formula in D55 must reference all three subtotals: D27 (Needs), D45 (Wants), and D53 (Financial Goals). Use cell references with the addition operator.
Your formula in D55 needs two addition operators (+) to add the three subtotals together.
Cell D55 needs to be formatted as currency. Select the cell, go to Format > Number > Currency.

objectives.title: Remaining Funds
objectives.description:
In cell D56, write a formula that subtracts your Total Spending (D55) from your Estimated Monthly Net Pay (C9). This shows how much money is left over (or how much you are over budget). Format the cell as currency.


In cells E55 and E56, write formulas that divide each row's dollar amount by your Estimated Monthly Net Pay using the absolute row reference C$9. Format both cells as percentages.


EXAMPLE:

[Total Spending] / [Estimated Monthly Net Pay]

[Remaining Funds] / [Estimated Monthly Net Pay]

resources.title: Video06.02
resources.transcript_summary:
This video covers two calculations: remaining funds and percentage totals. For remaining funds, you write a subtraction formula: your estimated monthly net pay minus your total monthly spending. This tells you how much money is left over (or over budget). In the example, about $1,900 remains, which ideally should be allocated further into your budget categories.

For the percentage row, instead of rewriting the division formula, you can just copy the percentage cell from above and paste it down. Because the formula uses a relative reference for the numerator (which shifts to the new row) and an absolute reference for the denominator (C$9, which stays locked on monthly net pay), it automatically calculates correctly. The total and remaining percentages should add up to 100%. Make sure all dollar amounts are formatted as currency and remove any extra borders, then evaluate.

sections.title: Reflections and Notes
sections.description: about spreadsheets, about budgeting, and about using AI as a learning tool. Strong reflections go beyond "it was good" or "I learned a lot." They describe specific moments, challenges, or realizations.

objectives.title: Notes
objectives.description:
You must complete the "Notes" section for at least EIGHT items in your budget. Focus on the ones that are the highest dollar amounts or most general. For example, housing, entertainment, vehicle, etc....


Include notes that help your teacher and an AI to understand the dollar amount. For example; the year, make, and model of a car. The number of rooms, SQFT, and if you have roommates for housing. Also what you will do with your entertainment or travel funds.

resources.title: Video 07.01
resources.transcript_summary:
This video explains the notes column requirements. You need at least eight notes total across all three sections (needs, wants, and savings), with at least two in each section. Notes should help your teacher and the AI understand why each expense is realistic. For example, if your housing says $2,367, a note like "one-bedroom apartment" explains the cost. If you're splitting rent, note that too.

The video warns you not to delete the section headers or totals rows, because the evaluator counts cells with content in the notes column across a fixed range. If you remove headers, the count will be off and you won't get full credit. Add descriptive notes like the type of car for a car payment, what your entertainment covers, or details about your savings goals.

sections.title: Teacher Graded
sections.description: This section is reviewed for the quality and thoughtfulness of your work, not just whether you completed each step. The focus is on whether your budget tells a realistic story, whether your calculations are accurate, and whether your reflections show genuine thought related to what you learned.

objectives.title: Budget Realism
objectives.description: Your budget should tell a believable financial story. The career you chose, the location you picked, the salary you researched, and the expenses you listed should all connect logically. A realistic budget is not about being perfect. It is about showing that you thought carefully about what life actually costs for someone in your situation.

resources.title: Video 08.01 & 02 & 03
resources.transcript_summary:
This video covers the final submission and grading process. Before submitting, review your work: Are your budget values based on real research or just guesses? Do your items actually reflect needs vs. wants vs. savings? Is the math correct? Are your reflections thorough and on-topic? These three teacher/AI-graded tasks are worth about 120 out of 300 points, so quality matters more than just completion.

When you click "Turn In Assignment," the AI reviews your work (usually within 2 minutes, but it can take longer if the system is busy). You'll see feedback and scores for reflection quality and completeness. If you want to improve your score, click "Unsubmit," make changes based on the feedback, and resubmit. The video notes that getting a perfect 100% is difficult since AI grading is subjective. If you're in the 90% range, submit it and talk to your teacher about earning the remaining points rather than endlessly resubmitting.

data.user_prompt:
Consider the notes information when determining realism.

`Grading Criteria`

1) The annual gross income entered in the spreadsheet should be a reasonable salary for the stated career and location. An entry-level teacher in rural Kansas earning $200,000 would not be realistic, just as a software engineer in San Francisco earning $25,000 would not be. The salary does not need to be exact, but it should fall within a believable range for the career and geographic area the student selected.

2) The effective tax rate should be a plausible combined federal and state rate for the income level and state listed. For most early-career salaries, this typically falls between 15% and 35%. A rate outside this range is not automatically wrong but should make sense given the specific circumstances. A 0% rate or a rate above 50% would indicate a misunderstanding.

3) The needs listed in the budget should reflect genuine essential expenses that a person in the stated location would realistically face. Housing costs should be roughly appropriate for the city or region. Other needs like groceries, transportation, utilities, and insurance should appear and their amounts should be within a reasonable range, not wildly high or suspiciously low.

4) The wants listed should be non-essential lifestyle expenses that are distinct from needs. Items like streaming subscriptions, dining out, gym memberships, hobbies, and personal spending are appropriate. If a student lists something as a want that most people would consider a need (like health insurance), or lists needs disguised as wants to game the percentages, the categorization should be evaluated critically.

5) The financial goals should include at least an emergency fund contribution and ideally additional goals like retirement savings, debt repayment, or a specific savings target. The monthly amounts should be realistic for the income level. Setting aside $5,000 per month on a $40,000 salary, or $2 per month toward retirement, would both suggest a lack of careful thought.

objectives.title: Reflection Quality
objectives.description: Your three reflections are a chance to show what you actually took away from this project. Strong reflections describe specific things you learned, challenges you faced, or decisions you made. They go beyond general statements and show that you are thinking critically about your own learning.

data.user_prompt:
`Grading Criteria`

1) The spreadsheet reflection should identify specific spreadsheet skills or concepts the student encountered during the project. Strong responses name particular skills like writing formulas, using SUM, applying number formatting, or working with absolute references, and describe what was challenging or new about them. Responses that only say "I learned a lot about spreadsheets" without any specifics do not demonstrate meaningful reflection.

2) The 50/30/20 reflection should show that the student engaged with the budgeting process itself, not just the mechanics of entering numbers. Strong responses discuss specific tradeoffs they made, surprises they encountered about the cost of living, or how close their budget came to the 50/30/20 targets and why. A response that simply restates the rule without connecting it to their own budget does not demonstrate reflection.

3) The AI reflection should describe a specific interaction the student had with an AI tool during the project. Strong responses explain what they asked for, what the AI provided, and how they used or evaluated that information. The response should show awareness that AI is a tool to support thinking, not a replacement for it. A vague statement like "AI helped me" without describing what happened does not meet this expectation.

4) All three reflections should be written in the student's own voice and contain enough detail to show genuine engagement. Each reflection should be at least 25 words and should read as a thoughtful response rather than a rushed sentence written to meet a minimum requirement.

objectives.title: Accuracy and Completeness
objectives.description: The 50/30/20 rule only works if items are placed in the right category. This task checks whether your needs, wants, and financial goals are properly sorted and whether your overall budget shows an intentional plan rather than random numbers. The pie chart configuration is included here as well.

resources.title: Video 08.01 & 02 & 03
resources.transcript_prompt: Review the transcript, then summarize it for high school students. Start with; This video is a tutorial on how to ......

data.user_prompt:
`Grading Criteria`

1) Every item in the Needs section (B12:B26) should be a genuine essential expense, meaning something the student could not reasonably go without. Common needs include housing, groceries, utilities, transportation, health insurance, phone service, and minimum debt payments. If luxury or lifestyle items appear in the Needs column, the categorization is inaccurate.

2) Every item in the Wants section (B30:B44) should be a discretionary or lifestyle expense. These are things the student enjoys or desires but could reduce or eliminate without jeopardizing basic safety or stability. Items like dining out, streaming services, vacations, and hobby spending belong here. If essential expenses appear in the Wants column to manipulate the percentages, that should be noted.

3) Every item in the Financial Goals section (B48:B52) should represent a savings or debt-reduction goal. Emergency fund contributions, retirement savings, student loan payments, and targeted savings goals are appropriate. Recurring monthly expenses like rent or subscriptions do not belong in this section.

4) The overall budget should show intentional planning. The three category percentages in column E should roughly approach the 50/30/20 targets, though they do not need to match exactly. What matters is that the student made thoughtful decisions about allocation. A budget where one category consumes 90% of income while another sits at 1% suggests the student did not engage with the balancing process, unless the reflections explain and justify the imbalance.

5) The spreadsheet should contain a pie chart that displays three slices representing Needs, Wants, and Financial Goals. The chart title should follow the format "50/30/20: [Student Name]" using the student's actual name from cell C2. The chart should include percentage labels on each slice so the visual breakdown is easy to read. The legend should be positioned on the right or left side with the title on the opposite side. The chart must be positioned and scaled so it fits directly to the right of the Income Profile section at the top of the spreadsheet.
